paras: The killing of Richard Dukes was a night attack in early July 1903 near River Junction in which a party of Black and white men tried to kill Cebe Dukes, a Black man, and then shot his father, Richard Dukes, to death and burned his house. Cebe Dukes escaped with a shoulder wound, and the only report found, a brief item in the Savannah Morning News, gave no motive and named no attackers.

On a "Thursday night" before 7 July 1903, probably 2 July, a "party of negroes and white men" attacked the house of Cebe Dukes, who lived about five miles from River Junction, "with the intention of killing him." Dukes ran out the back door into the woods and escaped, though he was shot in the shoulder as he fled.

The party, which the report called "the mob," then went to the nearby house of his father, Richard Dukes, and fired into it. Richard Dukes also fled out the back, but "two loads of buckshot and several bullets" struck him and killed him instantly. The attackers then set his house on fire, and it burned with all his belongings. His wife had hidden between the mattresses on the bed and was nearly burned with the building.
The report named none of the attackers and mentioned no arrests, inquest or official response, and no later report of any of these was found.

The Savannah Morning News ran the account on page 6 of its 7 July 1903 issue under the headline "MOB'S MURDEROUS WORK," without a dateline or a state for River Junction. The item was a plain narrative that identified Cebe Dukes as "a negro" and the attackers as a mixed party, offering neither an accusation against the victims nor any comment on the killing. No other report of the attack, in either white or Black newspapers, appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Killing of Richard Dukes
bases: A1 describes a night attack by an armed 'party' it calls 'the mob' on two Black households, with one man killed, one wounded and a house burned, but reports no accusation, custody or claim of punishment.

A1 reports Richard Dukes shot dead by a 'party of negroes and white men' acting without any authority, but gives no number of attackers and no accusation, motive or claim of justice, so the pretext element cannot be judged from the single report.
A1, an undatelined item in the Savannah Morning News, is the only report found in either press.
